ARCHITECTURAL COMPLEX OF THE MUSEUM  
The museum complex consists of the Winter Palace, Small Hermitage, Old Hermitage, Hermitage Theatre, New Hermitage, and Reserve (Storage) House (30–38 Dvortsovaya Embankment); Eastern Wing and the Arch of the General Staff Building (6–8 Palace Square); Menshikov Palace (15 Universitetskaya Embankment); “Staraya Derevnya” Centre for Restoration, Conservation and Storage (37 Zausadebnaya Street); Imperial Porcelain Manufactory Museum, located on the premises of the Imperial Porcelain Manufactory Public Company (151 Prospekt Obukhovskoy Oborony) and Stock Exchange (4 Birzhevaya Square).

MUSEUM BUILDINGS  
Winter Palace. 1754–1762  
Architect, Francesco Bartolomeo Rastrelli  
Reconstructed by Vasily Stasov after a fire in 1837

Small Hermitage. 1763–1775  
Architects, Yuri Velten and Jean-Baptiste Vallin de la Mothe

Old (Large) Hermitage. 1771–1787  
Architect, Yuri Velten

Hermitage Theatre. 1783–1787  
Architect, Giacomo Quarenghi

New Hermitage. 1842–1851  
Designed by architect Leo von Klenze; constructed under supervision of architects Vasily Stasov and Nikolay Efimov

Reserve (Storage) House of the Winter Palace. 1726–1742, 1830, 1878  
Architects, Domenico Trezzini (?), Carlo Giuseppe Trezzini and Nikolay Bekker

Menshikov Palace. 1710–1727  
Architects, Giovanni Mario Fontana and Georg Schedel

General Staff Building (former Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Ministry of Finance building). 1819–1829  
Architect, Carlo Rossi

“Staraya Derevnya” Centre for Restoration, Conservation and Storage  
Completion of the first phase – 2003, completion of the second phase – 2012

Summary

The Winter Palace was built by Bartolomeo Francesco Rastrelli in 1762 as the main residence of the Russian Emperors and Empresses and served the Romanovs for one hundred and fifty years – from Catherine the Great to Nicholas II. The renowned nineteenth-century Russian poet Vasily Zhukovsky wrote: “The greatness of the Winter Palace and its architecture reflect the mighty of the people… for us it represents the national Russian idea”. For a century and a half the Winter Palace was a venue for almost all of the most significant events of Russian history.

After the fall of the Romanov dynasty in February 1917 the Prime Minister of the Provisional Government Alexander Kerensky moved to the former residence together with his staff and guards. On 25 October 1917 the Provisional Government ministers, who were having their regular meeting in the Winter Palace, were arrested here by the Bolsheviks.
